justice: Most street space is allocated to motor vehicles, while no visible dedicated sidewalk is provided for pedestrians.
A construction fence occupies the right edge of the roadway, further reducing usable space for non-motorized users.
There are no visible curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or other barrier-free elements, limiting accessibility for diverse users.
safety: A large red truck, a black sedan, and a blue truck are all using the same carriageway as a small slow-moving three-wheeler, creating speed and size conflicts.
There is no visible bike lane, shoulder, or pedestrian refuge, so vulnerable road users would need to share space directly with motor traffic.
Roadside construction debris and the fenced excavation/canal edge create roadside hazards and reduce recovery space if users deviate from the travel lane.
livability: The street is dominated by industrial-style buildings, utility poles, and vehicle movement, with little evidence of active public life or social amenities.
No benches, bus stops, shopfront activity, or public gathering spaces are visible along the corridor.
The adjacent construction area, rubble, and fenced channel reduce the sense of neighborhood vitality and everyday usability.
sustainability: There is no visible public transit stop, protected cycling facility, or pedestrian-priority infrastructure to support low-carbon travel choices.
Tree canopy is extremely limited, offering little green infrastructure or shade-based climate adaptation.
The corridor's design appears vehicle-oriented, and the exposed construction/engineered channel edge suggests a hardscape environment with low ecological quality.
aesthetics: Long stretches of overhead utility wires and poles create visual clutter across the sky view.
Construction fencing, rubble piles, and unfinished roadside edges reduce visual quality.
The street has some visual order from straight road alignment and consistent industrial building forms, but overall appearance remains harsh and utilitarian.
comfort: There is almost no visible shade from trees or canopies, so thermal comfort would be poor in hot weather.
No seating, resting points, or pedestrian amenities are present, reducing physical comfort for people outside vehicles.
Shared exposure to moving trucks and cars on an open industrial road likely creates psychological discomfort for pedestrians and cyclists.
walkability: A continuous sidewalk is not visible on either side, making walking routes unclear and likely unsafe.
The right side is blocked by a construction fence and canal edge, while the left side has rough edges and debris rather than a pedestrian path.
No marked crosswalks, pedestrian signals, shade, or active frontages are visible to support convenient walking.
bikeability: There is no visible bike lane, painted shoulder, or physical protection for cyclists.
Cyclists would need to mix with heavy vehicles such as the red truck and other motor traffic in a narrow shared corridor.
No bicycle parking, cycle markings, or intersection treatments are visible to support safe and convenient cycling.
